scenes.heading: Graceful Shutdown
scenes.narration: Let's spend a minute on graceful shutdown, the discipline that turns every deploy from dropped requests into an invisible rollover.

scenes.heading: What graceful shutdown means
items: Stop accepting new work when the signal arrives
Drain in-flight requests within a deadline
Release dependencies in reverse startup order
scenes.narration: Every push to production sends SIGTERM to old pods. The naive response, exiting immediately, drops every in-flight request and can leave databases in an inconsistent state. Graceful shutdown is the alternative: stop taking new work, let the work you already accepted finish within a bounded deadline, then release resources in a safe order. In Go it's built from signal.NotifyContext, http.Server.Shutdown, and context.WithTimeout.

scenes.heading: The shutdown sequence
steps: Close consumers, then DB, then caches
scenes.narration: The order matters. The signal cancels the root context. First flip the readiness probe to five oh three so the load balancer stops routing new traffic, and pause briefly for that change to propagate. Then call Shutdown with a bounded context: the accept loop stops, idle connections close, and active handlers drain while ListenAndServe returns the ErrServerClosed sentinel. Only after handlers drain do you close what they depended on, in reverse of startup order.

scenes.heading: A complete graceful server
scenes.narration: signal.NotifyContext converts SIGINT and SIGTERM into an ordinary cancellable context. ListenAndServe runs in a goroutine, and a clean shutdown surfaces as ErrServerClosed, which we deliberately ignore. Main blocks on ctx.Done, then drains with a twenty-five second bounded Shutdown, comfortably under Kubernetes' grace period. If the drain overruns the deadline, we fall back to Close so the process always terminates.

scenes.text: Catching SIGTERM alone isn't enough on Kubernetes — the load balancer may still route traffic. Fail readiness first, then drain.
scenes.narration: The common trap: catching SIGTERM alone doesn't prevent dropped requests on Kubernetes, because the load balancer may keep routing for a moment after the signal. You must also fail the readiness probe first and wait for endpoint propagation. And keep the deadline shorter than the grace period, or SIGKILL will truncate your drain.
